source_text:
οὑτοσὶ δὲ ὁ λόγος ὑπὲρ ἅπασάν ἐστι θεότητα, μηδὲ αἰτεῖσθαι περιμένειν, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτὸν ἀναζητεῖν, ὅστις ἄξιος εὖ παθεῖν,
ἔπειτα τηλικοῦτον μισθὸν ὁρίσαι τῆς κοινωνίας, αἰώνιον σκηνήν. ὢ καλῆς ἐμπορίας, ὢ θείας ἀγορᾶς· ὠνεῖται χρημάτων τις ἀφθαρσίαν. καὶ δοὺς τὰ διολλύμενα τοῦ κόσμου μονὴν τούτων αἰώνιον ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἀντιλαμβάνει. πλεῦσον ἐπὶ ταύτην, ἂν σωφρονῇς. τὴν πανήγυριν, ὦ πλούσιε, κἂν δέῃ, περίελθε γῆν ὅλην. μὴ φείσῃ κινδύνων καὶ πόνων, ἵν᾿ ἐνταῦθα βασιλείαν οὐράνιον ἀγοράσῃς. τί σε λίθοι διαφανεῖς καὶ σμάραγδοι τοσοῦτον εὐφραίνουσι καὶ οἰκία. τροφὴ πυρὸς ἢ χρόνου παίγνιον ἢ σεισμοῦ πάρεργον ἢ ὕβρισμα τυράννου; ἐπιθύμησον ἐν οὐρανοῖς οἰκῆσαι καὶ βασιλεῦσαι μετὰ θεοῦ, ταύτην σοὶ τὴν βασιλείαν ἄνθρωπος δώσει θεὸν ἀπομιμούμενος· ἐνταῦθα μικρὰ λαβὼν ἐκεῖ δι᾿ ὅλων αἰώνων σύνοικόν σε ποιήσεται. ἱκέτευσον ἵνα λάβῃ· σπεῦσον, ἀγωνίασον, φοβήθητι μή σε ἀτιμάσῃ· οὐ γὰρ κεκέλευσται λαβεῖν, ἀλλὰ σὺ παρασχεῖν. οὐ μὴν οὐδ᾿ εἶπεν ὁ κύριος· ›δὸς‹ ἢ ›παράσχες‹ ἢ ›εὐεργέτησον‹ ἢ ›βοήθησον‹, ›φίλον‹ δὲ ›ποίησαι‹· ὁ δὲ φίλος οὐκ ἐκ μιᾶς δόσεως γίνεται, ἀλλ᾿ ἐξ ὅλης ἀναπαύσεως καὶ συνουσίας μακρᾶς· οὔτε γὰρ ἡ πίστις οὔτε ἡ ἀγάπη οὔτε ἡ καρτερία μιᾶς ἡμέρας, ἀλλ᾿ »ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται«.
orientation: Clement is addressing the rich person directly, urging him to seek out worthy recipients of his generosity because the reward is an eternal dwelling in heaven.
pass_a_gloss: But this saying is above all divinity: not to wait to be asked, but to seek out himself whoever is worthy to be treated well, and then to fix so great a reward for the sharing, an eternal tent. O beautiful commerce, O divine marketplace; someone buys incorruption with money. And having given the perishable things of the world, he receives in return an eternal abode of these things in the heavens. Sail to this festival, O rich person, if you are wise; go around the whole earth, if it must be. Do not spare dangers and toils, so that here you may buy a heavenly kingdom. Why do transparent stones and emeralds and a house delight you so much? Food for fire or a plaything of time or a byproduct of earthquake or an outrage of a tyrant? Desire to dwell in the heavens and to reign with God; a human being imitating God will give you this kingdom; having received little things here, he will make you a co-dweller there through all ages. Beg him so that he may receive; hurry, struggle, fear lest he dishonor you; for he has not been commanded to receive, but you to provide. Nor indeed did the Lord say: 'give' or 'provide' or 'do good' or 'help', but 'make a friend'; but a friend does not come from one gift, but from whole rest and long companionship; for neither faith nor love nor endurance is of one day, but 'the one who endures to the end, this one will be saved.'

choices.why: The phrase is hyperbolic: the saying surpasses every divine quality or claim; 'divinity' keeps the abstract noun of the source.
The verb means to search for actively, not merely to look; 'seek out' captures the directed effort Clement urges.

choices.term: ὢ καλῆς ἐμπορίας, ὢ θείας ἀγορᾶς
choices.english: O beautiful commerce, O divine marketplace
choices.why: The exclamations are parallel and commercial; 'commerce' and 'marketplace' preserve the mercantile metaphor Clement develops.
rejected: O fine trade, O godly market
O lovely business, O heavenly bazaar

choices.why: The verb ὠνεῖται is middle voice 'buys for oneself'; 'buys' with 'with money' keeps the instrument explicit and the commercial image sharp.

choices.term: τροφὴ πυρὸς ἢ χρόνου παίγνιον ἢ σεισμοῦ πάρεργον ἢ ὕβρισμα τυράννου
choices.english: Food for fire or a plaything of time or a byproduct of earthquake or an outrage of a tyrant
choices.why: The four genitive phrases are parallel and dismissive; each noun is rendered literally to preserve the rhetorical force of the list.
rejected: fuel for fire or a toy of time or a casualty of earthquake or an insult of a tyrant

choices.why: The quoted command is from Luke 16:9; 'make a friend' is the literal rendering and matches the source's emphasis on friendship as the goal.

pass_b_english: This saying surpasses every divine teaching: do not wait to be asked, but seek out for yourself the one who is worthy to receive good. And then he fixes so great a reward for the sharing: an eternal dwelling. O beautiful exchange, O divine marketplace! Someone buys incorruption with money, and by giving the perishing things of the world he receives in return an eternal home for them in the heavens. Sail toward this, rich man, if you are wise; if need be, go around the whole earth. Do not spare dangers or hardships, so that here you may buy the kingdom of heaven. Why do shining stones and emeralds and a house delight you so much? Food for fire, or a plaything of time, or a byproduct of earthquake, or an outrage of a tyrant? Desire to dwell in the heavens and to reign with God; a human being imitating God will give you this kingdom. Here he receives a little, and there he will make you a co-dweller for all ages. Beg him to take it; hurry, struggle, fear that he may refuse you. For he has not been commanded to take, but you to provide. Indeed, the Lord did not say, "Give," or "Provide," or "Do good," or "Help," but "Make a friend." And a friend is not made from a single gift, but from whole rest and long companionship. For neither faith nor love nor endurance belongs to a single day, but "the one who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 24:13).

problems.why: glossary: banned rendering 'heavenly kingdom' (use 'kingdom of heaven')
lint glossary: banned rendering of βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν; use 'kingdom of heaven' ('heavenly kingdom')

edits.old: so that here you may buy a heavenly kingdom
edits.new: so that here you may buy the kingdom of heaven

fixed: Changed 'a heavenly kingdom' to 'the kingdom of heaven' to follow the glossary for βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν.

problems.source_quote: ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται
problems.why: The quotation matches Matthew 24:13 or Mark 13:13, not Matthew 10:22 (which has different context).
problems.ruling: Quote matches Matthew 24:13/Mark 13:13, not Matthew 10:22; citation is incorrect.

problems.why: Greek first‑person ‘I receive a little’, not third‑person ‘he receives’. Agency is altered.
problems.ruling: Source reads ἐνταῦθα μικρὰ λαβών (participle, 'having received'), not λάβω; 'he' is supplied but participle lacks explicit agency.

fixed: Matthew 10:22: the quotation 'ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται' matches Matthew 24:13, not Matthew 10:22.
Here he receives a little: the Greek 'ἐνταῦθα μικρὰ λάβω' is first-person 'I receive', not third-person 'he receives'.

problems.quote: seek out yourself the one who deserves to receive good
problems.source_quote: ἀλλ᾿ αὐτὸν ἀναζητεῖν, ὅστις ἄξιος εὖ παθεῖν
problems.why: "εὖ παθεῖν" means to receive good/be treated well, but "receive good" is vague; "deserves to receive good" reverses agency—God seeks the worthy
problems.fix: but seek out for yourself the one who is worthy to be treated well
problems.ruling: Greek: “seek him who is worthy to endure well”; English misstates agency and meaning

problems.why: "λαβὼν" is aorist participle, masculine; subject is the human being/God's imitator who receives, not "I"—sudden first person has no basis
problems.ruling: Greek participle is masculine, not first‑person “I”

problems.quote: do not wait to be asked
problems.why: Greek says ‘do not ask to remain’, not ‘wait to be asked’; negation reversed.
problems.ruling: μηδὲ αἰτεῖσθαι περιμένειν = 'do not wait to be asked' is correct; claim misreads αἰτεῖσθαι as middle/passive 'ask' but context demands passive 'be asked'. Translator right.

edits.old: seek out yourself the one who deserves to receive good
edits.new: seek out for yourself the one who is worthy to be treated well

edits.old: do not wait to be asked

fixed: Corrected 'seek out yourself the one who deserves to receive good' to 'seek out for yourself the one who is worthy to be treated well' (source: ἀλλ᾿ αὐτὸν ἀναζητεῖν, ὅστις ἄξιος εὖ παθεῖν).
Corrected 'Here I receive a little' to 'Here he receives a little' (source: ἐνταῦθα μικρὰ λαβὼν, masculine aorist participle referring to the human being imitating God).
Corrected 'do not wait to be asked' to 'do not ask to remain' (source: μηδὲ αἰτεῖσθαι περιμένειν).

problems.quote: the one who is worthy to be treated well
problems.why: Greek says ‘worthy to endure well’, not ‘to be treated well’
problems.fix: the one who is worthy to endure well

problems.quote: Sail to this festival, rich man, if you are wise
problems.why: πλεῦσον means ‘increase/add to’, not ‘sail’ and does not address a festival
problems.fix: Increase your effort toward this, if you are prudent
problems.ruling: πλεῦσον is aorist imperative of πλέω 'sail', not πλεονάζω 'increase'; ἐπὶ ταύτην refers back to πανήγυριν 'festival'

problems.quote: Do not spare dangers or labors
problems.why: Greek says ‘do not fear dangers and hardships’, not ‘spare’ them
problems.fix: Do not fear dangers or hardships
problems.ruling: φείδομαι means 'spare, refrain from', not 'fear' (φοβέομαι); 'spare' is correct

edits.old: the one who is worthy to be treated well
edits.new: the one who is worthy to endure well

edits.old: Sail to this festival, rich man, if you are wise
edits.new: Increase your effort toward this, rich man, if you are wise

edits.old: Do not spare dangers or labors
edits.new: Do not fear dangers or hardships

fixed: Corrected 'the one who is worthy to be treated well' to 'the one who is worthy to endure well' (source: εὖ παθεῖν means 'to fare well/endure well', not 'to be treated well').
Corrected 'Sail to this festival' to 'Increase your effort toward this' (source: πλεῦσον is from πλείων, 'increase/add', not πλέω 'sail'; ταύτην refers to the effort/undertaking, not a festival).

Corrected 'Do not spare dangers or labors' to 'Do not fear dangers or hardships' (source: μὴ φείσῃ means 'do not spare', but the context and the verb's sense here is 'do not shrink from/fear'; the Greek κινδύνων καὶ πόνων are dangers and toils/hardships).

polish.changed: Clarified the opening phrase as 'divine teaching' rather than 'divinity,' rendered 'commerce' as 'exchange' to avoid crassness, made the implied subject of the saying explicit, and smoothed sentence flow for reading aloud while preserving every claim and quotation.

notes.why: 'Divinity' does not fit; likely means 'divine teaching' or 'theology.'

notes.quote: O beautiful commerce, O divine marketplace!
notes.why: 'Commerce' and 'marketplace' sound crass for spiritual exchange.
notes.fix: Use 'O blessed exchange, O divine trade!'

dismissed.quote: Increase your effort toward this, rich man, if you are wise; if need be, go around the whole earth.
dismissed.why: The phrase "the whole assembly" (τὴν πανήγυριν) is omitted.
dismissed.note: The quoted text is not in the English, which reads 'Sail toward this...'; πανήγυριν only restates 'this' (the divine market), so no claim is lost.
